The challenges of data collection across the High North’s and the Baltic Sea region’s areas of interest only serve to underscore the value of space-based ISR and of its integration with other domains. In the maritime domain, for example, space-based surveillance would reduce and possibly negate any advantage a surface vessel currently has in maneuvering to avoid detection – and commercial providers already offer near constant coverage of specified areas. The use of software to provide an automated first pass of data – to reduce the human workload – also offers promise.57

conditions.58 There is a growing awareness of the issues posed by space debris – a byproduct of the deployment of orbital ISR – and the Kessler syndrome, where a space-debris event has a cascading impact.59 The increasing strategic relevance of space led NATO to identify space-domain awareness as a goal for the Alliance. This concept was originally defined by the United States Space Force as the capacity to identify, characterise and understand any factors that could potentially affect space operations.60 In addition to SSA, space-domain awareness therefore provides intelligence on potential threats – inadvertent and deliberate.61

The ever-increasing commercial use of space is both a benefit to and a potential problem for armed forces and defence ministries. Many commercial products are of military value and are fundamentally dual use. (Their ready availability, however, may mean that they could also be used by a rival.) Such commercial offerings predominate in low-Earth orbit (LEO), the result being that LEO – in space terms, at least – is increasingly cluttered and therefore poses a greater risk of collision. The military utility of commercial space has been evident in the war in Ukraine, where private actors and international agencies have provided satellite communications (SATCOM), internet connectivity and imagery to allow Ukrainian forces to better organise and respond to the Russian invasion.62
